posts.note: SXSW 2023 recap essay on Daniel Johnston; retrospective. One philosophical conditional about healers logged as borderline.
Capability checklist relayed from payer insiders; the list itself is descriptive. Two borderline items: a closing disclaimer and a footnote heuristic on pilot-to-contract conversion.
Verizon customer-service anecdote; one aphoristic AI automation claim in the opening line.
Transcript of a 2022-05-28 Clubhouse conversation with Sohaib Imtiaz, republished 2023-03-28. Two aggregate claims about mass shootings recurring; parenting advice is normative and not logged.
Reproduces the author's 2006 medical school personal statement with annotations. One GPT-4 adoption claim; one 2006 self-prediction quoted from the statement.

Satirical post on the Gag Clause Prohibition Compliance Attestation (GCPCA). Four items: the compliance standard, a parody 'national holiday' (sincere false), the quoted Dec 31, 2023 deadline, and the expectation of seeing kickback sizes.

Parody venture pitch plus statistics essay on regression to the mean and Bayes. Fictional pitch lines ('We promise to save you money') not logged as forecasts; one rhetorical closing claim logged as borderline.
Burst of AI/deepfake predictions in the intro; the CV body (most of the 5545 words) is retrospective and yielded nothing.

statements.quote: If we decide to accept illness that must be cured as the frame of reference, we will not succeed as healers.
statements.context: Closing reflection of a SXSW 2023 recap about Daniel Johnston, the indie musician with a psychotic illness who died of a heart attack. The author argues that if healers adopt a cure-the-illness frame rather than relieving suffering without judgment about its causes, they will fail as healers.
statements.note: Philosophical conditional about the profession; not a dated or checkable forecast. Borderline, logged for recall.

statements.quote: I'm not saying it's going to get you a contract, even if you have it all.
statements.context: Closing disclaimer after a bullet list of capabilities that Big Health payers (Blue Cross, United, CIGNA, Aetna, Humana) reportedly want from value-based behavioral health programs. The author declines to predict that having every listed capability yields a contract.
statements.confidence_phrase: I'm not saying it's going to
statements.note: Disclaimer that withholds a forecast rather than making one; logged for recall. Borderline.

statements.quote: The best predictor of a pilot turning into a contract and subsequently, a major program is the stability of leadership in the company.
statements.context: Footnote 1 of the payer value-based contracting guide. The author cautions that what payer insiders say they want and what they are allowed to sign can differ; from his own and colleagues' experience, a leadership change at the Big Health company kills pilots, so leadership stability predicts pilot-to-contract conversion.
statements.note: General experience-based heuristic about pilot conversion, not a dated call. Borderline.

statements.quote: I believe the revolution will be automated.
statements.context: Opening line of a short post praising the staff of a Brooklyn Verizon store. The author says he is a fan of AI and expects an automation-driven revolution, then pivots to celebrate human kindness.
statements.note: Vague aphoristic AI call (play on 'the revolution will not be televised'); low specificity.

statements.quote: We can know it's highly likely to happen again.
statements.context: Transcript of a May 28, 2022 live conversation with Dr. Sohaib Imtiaz after the Uvalde, Texas school shooting, republished 2023-03-28. The author says we cannot know in advance who the next mass shooter will be, but that another mass shooting is highly likely.
statements.note: Spoken 2022-05-28, republished 2023-03-28. Base-rate style claim that US mass shootings will recur.

statements.quote: the more people we have who feel adrift, unloved, uncared for, misunderstood, and enraged, the more likelihood is some of them are going to choose to express their rage with bullets.
statements.context: Same 2022 conversation on mass shootings. The author states a causal expectation: the more socially adrift and enraged people in the population, the higher the likelihood that some of them will commit shootings.
statements.confidence_phrase: the more likelihood is ... are going to
statements.note: Aggregate causal claim, not a dated forecast; from a 2022 conversation republished in 2023. Borderline.

statements.quote: And #GPT4 has made writing these things something no one will ever do again.
statements.context: Introduction to a post reproducing the author's 2006 medical school personal statement. He claims GPT-4 has ended the practice of applicants writing personal statements themselves.
statements.note: Absolute AI-adoption call ('no one will ever'); hyperbolic tone but reads as a sincere expectation.

statements.quote: I also have never had a moment of doubt that I should be a doctor, and that I will be a great one.
statements.context: Final line of the author's 2006 personal statement to the University of Rochester School of Medicine and Dentistry, reproduced verbatim in 2023 with 'comments from the future'. The then-applicant predicts he will be a great doctor.
entities: University of Rochester School of Medicine and Dentistry
statements.note: Written in 2006, republished 2023-03-28; self-prediction about the author's own career. Coder may treat as historical or CONTROL. Borderline.

statements.quote: There is a new standard with which health insurers and group health insurance plans will have to comply.
statements.context: Opening of a satirical post proposing a 'National Gag Clause Remembrance Day'. The author announces the Gag Clause Prohibition Compliance Attestation (GCPCA) requirement under the Consolidated Appropriations Act, 2021, which health insurers and group health plans must meet.
entities: Departments of Labor, Health and Human Services, and the Treasury
statements.note: Restates an enacted legal requirement; the future element is payer compliance. Sincere despite the satirical frame of the post.

statements.quote: Something important is coming, a very special day, which will be a new national holiday.
statements.context: Satirical set-up: the author proposes that December 31, the annual GCPCA attestation deadline, become 'National Gag Clause Remembrance Day' in place of New Year's Eve.
statements.note: Parody. 'New national holiday' is a joke, not a real expectation.

statements.quote: The initial GCPCA must be submitted by December 31, 2023, for the period covering December 27, 2020 through December 31, 2023.
statements.context: Block quote from the National Law Review that the author relays as 'great news': group health plans and insurers must submit the first Gag Clause Prohibition Compliance Attestation to the Departments of Labor, HHS and Treasury by December 31, 2023, and then annually via the CMS webform.
entities: Departments of Labor, Health and Human Services, and the Treasury
statements.note: Quoted third party (National Law Review) stating a regulatory deadline; the author adopts it as fact. Regulatory calendar item rather than a forecast proper.

statements.quote: Every employer and payer has to do this. It's mandatory. Now I get to see how big the kickbacks really are!
statements.context: Closing of the gag clause post. The author expects that mandatory GCPCA attestations, which end the confidentiality of negotiated rates, will let him see the size of payer and PBM 'kickbacks'.
statements.note: Compound: mandatory compliance (statement of law) plus the expectation that disclosures will reveal kickback sizes. Exuberant tone; the underlying expectation reads sincere.

statements.quote: there is a fiduciary duty to uphold , and the time for scams is over.
statements.context: Closing of a parody pitch for a care-management company that would claim savings actually produced by regression to the mean among top-1% cost claimants. The author says Bayesian reasoning lets payers and fiduciaries see through such vendor claims, and declares the era of these scams over.
statements.note: Rhetorical declaration that vendor savings scams will end; not a dated call. Borderline. The space before the comma is in the source text.

statements.quote: GPT 3.5 will be, in like a month or two, what 8 bit Nintendo games were 20 years later. A source of amusement!
statements.context: Opening of a post about using GPT-4 to format the author's CV. He predicts GPT-3.5 will look like a retro curiosity within one to two months as GPT-4 supersedes it.
statements.horizon_text: in like a month or two
statements.note: Dated (1-2 months) call on GPT-3.5 obsolescence; metaphorical framing.

statements.quote: In fact, in the near future, this will no longer be a thing. The robots are placing us on the Internet at least, and there will be no such thing as a CV you have to manually put together.
statements.context: The author, who put off updating his CV for a year, predicts that manually assembled CVs will disappear in the near future because AI will generate them from people's online records.
statements.note: Compound: end of manual CVs plus AI auto-generation from online presence.

statements.quote: It will generate real CVs. It will generate fake CVs.
statements.context: Continues the CV prediction: AI ('the robots') will generate both real and fabricated CVs.
statements.note: Follows the 'near future' CV claim; AI-generated real and fake credentials.

statements.quote: The difference between the real the generated by hallucinations of artificial intelligence will be rapidly swept away.
statements.context: The author predicts that the distinction between real documents and AI-hallucinated ones will rapidly collapse.
statements.note: Garbled sentence in the source ('the real the generated'); quoted verbatim.

statements.quote: There will be no such thing as wire tap evidence without testimony in court—everything is deep fake, when it comes to defense attorneys.
statements.context: Extends the deepfake argument to the legal system: the author predicts wiretap recordings will no longer stand as evidence without live testimony because defense attorneys will call everything a deepfake.
statements.confidence_phrase: There will be no such thing
statements.note: AI/deepfake impact on court evidence; not dated.

statements.quote: Everything you can imagine cracking as a system by just throwing AI generated content at it has already been broken by the time you figure out what it is by somebody slightly more devious and with more free time than you.
statements.context: In the same AI-disruption passage, the author claims any system exploitable with AI-generated content gets broken before others notice; present-perfect framing of an ongoing and continuing dynamic.
statements.note: Present-perfect general claim about a continuing pattern; borderline forward-looking. Logged for recall.

statements.quote: 90% of the lawyers are out of a job.
statements.context: In a burst of AI-disruption predictions, the author asserts, in rhetorical present tense, that 90 percent of lawyers lose their jobs as AI-generated content breaks document-based systems.
statements.note: Numeric call (90%) written in present tense as a future certainty; hyperbolic tone but reads sincere. No date given.

statements.quote: Mid level management, it's been nice knowing you.
statements.context: Same passage: the author predicts AI eliminates mid-level management jobs, immediately after the '90% of the lawyers' line.
statements.note: Farewell framing implies job elimination; hyperbolic tone, reads sincere.

statements.quote: The things that are valuable will be in person, ever onward.
statements.context: The author predicts that as digital content becomes fakeable, value shifts permanently to in-person interactions.
statements.note: Open-ended structural claim.

statements.quote: Paper is going to make a huge comeback for anything important when it comes to documents.
statements.context: The author predicts a return to paper for important documents as a response to AI-generated fakes.
statements.note: Analog comeback claim; no date.

statements.quote: There will be an Audit Trails. There will be metadata. Polaroid film!
statements.context: Continues the anti-fake prediction list: audit trails, metadata and analog photography (Polaroid film) will return as authenticity guarantees.
statements.note: Compound list of three; verbatim grammar ('an Audit Trails').

statements.quote: So much that isn't digital will have to be popular again.
statements.context: Summary line of the analog-comeback predictions: non-digital media and documents will regain popularity.
statements.note: Restates the paper and in-person comeback claims.

statements.quote: When anything on the Internet could be fake, then maybe we will have to be skeptical.
statements.context: The author judges the coming fake-content era 'probably good' because it may force general skepticism toward online content.
statements.note: Hedged conditional about the social response to AI fakes.
